endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: For autonomous AI, a rigorous ongoing monitoring program is imperative to detect and rectify errors promptly (11).

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Higher risk solutions require more frequent review cycles and enhanced escalation pathways.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: CDRH recognizes that there may be a variety of different approaches to postmarket monitoring of GenAI-enabled devices, and that the scope, frequency, and level of evidence of such approaches might vary in proportion to the risk profile of the device.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Ongoing post-deployment monitoring should be riskbased and scaled to your setting.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Risks should be identified and documented throughout the pilot deployment of the health AI solution, risk assessment methods should be in place, and a mechanism should exist to act upon them.

endorsements.title: Developing, Purchasing, Implementing and Monitoring AI Tools in Radiology: Practical Considerations. A Multi-Society Statement from the ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR and RSNA
endorsements.quote: Strategies for real-world monitoring of AI in clinical practice should take into account the type of AI model being used and the risk to patient safety if the model performance declines.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in medicine: mitigating risks and maximizing benefits via quality assurance, quality control, and acceptance testing
endorsements.quote: The frequency of monitoring should be aligned with the risk that the tool poses (ie, higher risk should require more frequent audits).

endorsements.title: Establishing responsible use of AI guidelines: a comprehensive case study for healthcare institutions
endorsements.quote: A risk-based approach should be taken to this monitoring, such that those applications that potentially introduce greater risk to care outcomes are monitored more robustly than those with minimal or no risk to clinical outcomes.

endorsements.title: Integrating Generative AI Into Patient-Centered Clinical Decision Support: Viewpoint on Research and Practice Considerations
endorsements.quote: Organizations should establish clear triggers for reassessment—such as major guideline updates, new evidence affecting care recommendations, demographic changes in the patient population, the passage of time, or early signals of performance deterioration—and establish a reassessment frequency based on the clinical risk and operational impact of the GenAI-supported application [ 84 85 ].

endorsements.title: Ethical oversight of AI-driven paediatric trials: a proactive, risk-sensitive interim review model
endorsements.quote: In this model, the IRB requires scheduled interim reviews of AI-driven paediatric trials, and on-site audits where appropriate, with the timing and intensity of review calibrated to the level and type of risk, rather than relying solely on annual continuing review.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: Because review burden should be proportional to risk and novelty, we do not assume a single fixed evaluation time for all use cases.

endorsements.title: Regulating digital surgery to balance safety and innovation: a SAGES white paper
endorsements.quote: There is a need for periodic but consistent performance monitoring with predefined intervention thresholds, and many of these technologies should include PCCPs.

endorsements.title: A six-level clinical autonomy framework for artificial intelligence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: In dentistry, increasing decisional delegation must correspond to intensified validation, monitoring, and governance requirements ( 17 ).

endorsements.title: Mental Health Innovation Is Scaling Faster Than Accountability
endorsements.quote: The same obligations should not apply to all tools; they should intensify as tools move from general wellbeing support toward symptom interpretation, therapeutic guidance, crisis escalation, autonomous monitoring, or clinician-supervised treatment.

endorsements.title: A five-phase evaluation framework for diagnostic and predictive medical artificial intelligence
endorsements.quote: Operationalizing post-market surveillance requires a risk-stratified monitoring cadence, with high-risk diagnostic systems undergoing daily or weekly automated checks and lower-risk applications monitored on a monthly basis.

commentary.bottom_line: Fifteen sources endorse matching monitoring frequency and intensity to each AI tool's clinical risk, but no study supplied here tests whether risk-tiered monitoring detects more errors or uses staff time better than uniform monitoring. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory signaling rather than on comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: No study tests risk-scaled monitoring, and no study documents the hazard of under- or over-monitoring. The support consists of guidance, frameworks, commentaries, and one regulatory discussion paper. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement across sources does not substitute for a test of the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FDA device center's discussion paper states that postmarket monitoring scope, frequency, and level of evidence might vary in proportion to device risk, using permissive language. A surgical society white paper calls for predefined intervention thresholds and predetermined change control plans. These documents signal regulatory direction but do not impose a tiered monitoring requirement on health systems.

A multi-society radiology statement uses mandatory language for autonomous AI, stating that ongoing monitoring is needed to detect and correct errors promptly. This reasoning rests on the absence of a clinician check before output reaches the patient. No supplied study measures how often tiered monitoring catches errors before harm, so the size of any safety benefit remains unknown.

Several sources, including a CHAI playbook and a patient-facing video governance matrix, frame proportional review as a way to direct limited review effort toward higher-risk tools. No supplied study reports staffing hours, costs, or feasibility of tiered monitoring programs, so the resource savings described in these sources remain untested.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares risk-tiered monitoring with uniform monitoring on error detection, time to detection, patient harm, or staff effort. Studies are also needed on how to assign risk tiers reliably and on whether conditionally deployed or autonomous tools drift or fail at rates that justify more frequent review.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary lists demographic change in the patient population as a trigger for reassessment, which suggests that risk tiers may need to account for performance differences in these groups, but this has not been examined.
